content.summary_of_the_paper: In this study, the authors have demonstrated the multi-view evidential deep fusion is a promising approach for the interpretation of mammograms for the two tasks including breast density classification and lesion malignancy prediction (based on BIRADS). Using the two public datasets (VinDr-mammo and mini-DDSM), they empirically showed that the deep evidential neural network extracts features from each view of mammogram (L-CC, L-MLO, R-CC, R-MLO), followed by the fusion of the features using Dempster-Shafer evidence theory outperforms single-view model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
• Figure 1 describes well on how each fusion behaves. The figure is very useful to make the reviewer understand what they attempted.

Weakness
• The reviewer thinks the authors need to elaborate how the output labels are defined for density assessment. In section 3. Datasets, it seems the authors gives confusing definitions of density and BIRADS findings like “we categorized BI-RADS density scores into two separate categories: BI-RADS 2 and 3 as benign and BI-RADS 5 and 6 as malignant”. There is no description about what “Density A”, “Density B”, “Density C”, and “Density D” mean. Also, as the reviewer knows, benign or malignant classification can be confirmed with biopsy results not BIRADS scores. Even though the reviewer is not familiar with the two public datasets, the reviewer thinks the datasets should have biopsy information to annotate lesions whether malignant or benign. 
• As a preprocessing step, the authors segmented and removed the region of the pectoral muscle from MLO views. However, the authors did not explain how the segmentation model was developed (they just mentioned employed the prior work) and the review has a concern that important features can be removed from this preprocessing step. It might be useful to compare model performance using MLO views with and without this preprocessing step to confirm the benefit of this pectoral muscle removal. 
• How did you calculate precision/recall/F1-score for 4-class classification of breast density? Also, for breast cancer detection, researchers usually report AUC with sensitivity and specificity at different operating points to compare model performance. It might be more informative to provide AUC results for comparisons. 
• The reviewer thinks comparison of their proposed approach with the single-view result is unfair. This is because information that multi views contain is 4x larger than the one that the single view has. So, to demonstrate the benefit of using the proposed fusion strategy, they need to report performance of multi-view results with simple fusion approach like the average/maximum of 4 view scores, or max over mean values of each breast. 
• Are the results reported in this study based on patient/study level? How did you calculate performance when using single views? Did you assume that each study has only one view?
• What fusion strategy was used for results in Table 2? Are these results based on image level?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The main novelty that the authors tried to claim is they applied evidential deep learning approach to multi-view assessment of mammograms. As the reviewer knows, evidential deep learning is meaningful to quantify the uncertainty in the model predictions to develop trust-aware AI models. However, EDL used in this study is just another fusion method of multi-view scores without providing interpretable results. Also, there are many prior research works to combine prediction scores of multi views of mammogram to achieve performance like radiologists. In addition, the reviewer is not sure that all the results can be reproduced because of lack of details mentioned above as weakness.
content.summary_of_the_review: This study attempted to apply an interesting deep learning approach (evidential deep learning) to mammogram assessment tasks, but their claims are not novel and their experimental results need improving to make their claims more reliable.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors explore the use of the DST to integrate information from multiple mammogram views (CC+MLO and colateral breast) for two tasks: density assessment and BIRADS estimation.

Although the paper is well written, easy to easy and technically sound in most parts,
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well written, easy to easy and technically sound in most parts.
Explores many DNN backbones.
Explores multiple fusions strategies.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written, easy to easy and technically sound in most parts.

The technical novelty seems limited. 
Even in breast cancer, DST has already been used for information fusion, although maybe not on the exactly same task:
Classifier Fusion Using Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence to Predict Breast Cancer Tumors
https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4142650?arnumber=4142650

Two-step evidential fusion approach for accurate breast region segmentation in mammograms
https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1049/iet-ipr.2018.5325
content.summary_of_the_review:
Besides the limited novelty, the paper missed doing a reasonable comparison with the SOTA, both theoretically and experimentally.
Additionally, the lack of cross-dataset evaluation is also a missed opportunity to explore the generalization in more real-life settings.

Minor details:
-"We pre-processed the mammograms using a minimum bounding box which captures only the mammogram and then, normalized each
mammogram using a min-max scaler." 
If this was this performed manually, the impact of the work is decreased.
-the differences between LEF and VS-LEF should be better explained.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript aims to improve the accuracy of mammography interpretation through the effective utilization of multiple views. The authors declare two contributions: a) they empirically investigate the effectiveness of pre-trained CNN as feature extractors for mammography images; b) they proposed an evidential-based fusion strategy; c) they conduct experiments on the effectiveness of all proposed fusion strategies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- This paper is organized and presented in a clean manner.
- The introduction about mammography and breast cancer is well-written. It provides sufficient background on the clinical significance of the BI-RADS and density prediction tasks.

Major concerns:
- [Generalizability] The proposed method is designed for a particular application (mammography interpretation). No further evidence is provided on whether this fusion strategy generalizes to other multi-view/multi-modal tasks. Compare to ICLR which focuses on generalizable ML discovery, this work fits better with other domain-specific conferences such as MICCAI and MIDL.
- [Novelty] This work lacks technical novelty. See the next section for details.
- [Baseline] No comparisons against multi-view baselines are presented. See the next section for details.

Minor concerns:
- The abstract is too long. Please consider moving some content to the introduction.
- The importance of evidential fusion is not well-explained. It's unclear how evidential fusion is connected to trust-aware ML.
- There seems to be no explicit definition of "evidential layer", which is the core component in view-wise fusion strategy.
- Regarding the task formulation, what's the reason for excluding BIRADS 0, 1, and 4?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
[Clarity] The clarity of this work is satisfactory.

[Quality] Experiments were conducted to support the claims in the paper. There is no major issue with the experimental setups. However, the selection of baselines is questionable. In Table 3, the authors compare the proposed multi-view model with the single-view model. The improved performance is in fact well-expected since for many cases cancer will be visible only in one of the four images. Instead of comparing against single-view models, the author should compare their method against other multi-view models such as the ones mentioned in the related work section.  

[Novelty] This work lacks novelty. First, many prior works have already investigated the effectiveness of transfer learning for mammography interpretation [1,2]. Second, the evidential fusion strategy is a direct application of a previously proposed method [3]. The only novelty, if any, comes from applying the uncertainty framework to a realistic clinical setting (breast cancer screening). However, there isn't much effort in connecting the uncertainty to clinical practice. For instance, on what samples does the model emit high uncertainty, and what does uncertainty mean in breast cancer screening?  

[Reproducibility] This work is trained and evaluated on public datasets. No code is provided for reproducibility.

[1] Falconí, Lenin G., María Pérez, and Wilbert G. Aguilar. "Transfer learning in breast mammogram abnormalities classification with mobilenet and nasnet." 2019 International Conference on Systems, Signals and Image Processing (IWSSIP). IEEE, 2019.
[2] Pardamean, Bens, et al. "Transfer learning from chest X-ray pre-trained convolutional neural network for learning mammogram data." Procedia Computer Science 135 (2018): 400-407.
[3] Han, Zongbo, et al. "Trusted multi-view classification." arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.02051 (2021).
content.summary_of_the_review: This manuscript applies evidential DL on a very relevant task. However, due to the generalizability and novelty, I recommend 5: marginally below the acceptance threshold.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors address two classification tasks of mammograms, one binary tasks (benign vs malignant) and one multiclass task of density classification. They experiment with different CNN architectures, which are pretrained and then fine tuned. Each sample has four different views available, and the authors explore different strategies to fuse the information of these views (concatenation of the input vs. combination of extracted features). They conclude that multiview processing is superior to using only a single view and that late-evidential fusion performs best.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Relevant application 
- Fusion strategies for multiview and multimodal data are a relevant topic
- Using two openly available datasets
- Perform two different classification tasks (one binary, one multiclass)
- Extensive evaluation of different architectures 

Weaknesses:
- Addressing one particular kind of data, there are no conclusions that can necessarily be drawn for any other kind of data
- Very limited novelty, and limited conclusions which can be drawn from the evaluations
- Experimental observations, I am lacking some theoretical understanding that explains the observed results
- Issues with reported numerical results
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- In the abstract the authors make the important point that for AI-based diagnostics and AI-assisted screening programs, explainable AI is of great importance to build trust in the biomedical community. It gives the impression as if the proposed method falls within the subject of explainable AI. However, it turns out that the interpretable part addresses the feature fusion step in the method, not the actual feature extraction by pretrained CNNs which are used. This is misleading in my opinion, as the real blackbox lies within the feature extraction of the CNNs (in particular when they are pretrained on data originating from an entirely different distribution). The authors include some visualization of saliency maps for two particular examples in Fig. 4&5 in the appendix, but this particular aspect is not enough addressed for the task as a whole to shed more light on the feature learning which would contribute to establish trust from a clinical and interpretable perspective.
- I’m lacking the motivation of how the Dempster-Shafer (please check the spelling of these two names throughout your paper) theory is helping the understanding of the classification at hand. Some keywords are introduced in section 2.2, but this section is not well connected to the other parts of the paper and requires reading Sensoy et al. (2018) to understand any context. It is unclear in what sense this part of the evaluated methods make the presented classification results more interpretable. Spend some time to introduce the reader to what the subject belief masses, the evidential layer, the Dempster combination rule are, and in what respect they influence the downstream classification task.
- I am also missing a final take-home message. In the Discussion and Conclusion section, the authors say that they have presented an approach that can be efficiently deployed in a clinical setting. Computational resources are usually sparse in a clinical setting, and this aspect is not at all addressed in the study. They say that “they empirically demonstrated their findings”, but it is not clear what these findings are exactly.
- In this section, they also address that they interpret the results by visualizing the gradients (is it really gradients you are visualizing?), but first of all this should be part of the results section, not the conclusions, and only two examples are shown, the results on the dataset are not further explored in this respect.
- The performance measures reported do not add up. I have not checked the entire table, but for example in Table 2, in the binary classification task (BI-RADS findings), if Precision is 0.92 and Recall is 0.92, then F1-Score, defined as the harmonic mean between the two, cannot be 0.94 but must also be 0.92; when Precision is 0.56 and Recall is 0.54, F-1 Score cannot be 0.50, etc, etc
- Even if this study is seen as an exploration contribution to study the influence of different network architectures, as a baseline it should be compared to a fully trained network, to show the superiority of using pretraining at all. Furthermore, it should state more clearly that the evaluated CNNs are pretrained on ImageNet (I assume), and address why pretraining on natural images is expected to be helpful for very different image data such as mammograms. Personally, I would find it more interesting to address different kinds of pretraining (self-supervised pretraining; pretraining on other X-Ray data; pretraining by solving another task, such as classifying if one view belongs to the same sample, i.e. if a particular L-CC view corresponds to a particular R-MLO view, etc) , then to address a large variety of architectures all pretrained on the same data.


Clarity:
- The application itself is well motivated, but overall the paper can be much improved in terms of clarity with respect to explaining how the use of EDL is beneficial for this task, in what way this study brings automated screening programs closer to actual use in clinical reality and reformulate the findings. 

Reproducibility:
- As far as I understand, no code is available. The data is preprocessed by segmentation and contrast adjustment. A validation set was used to tune hyperparameters, but as only one set of optimizer parameters is given for all experiments, I assume there are other hyperparameters which require tuning, that are not listed in the paper. The training-test-validation split is not provided.



Minor Comments:
- Abstract and Sect 1: “Dempster-Shafter”-> “Dempster–Shafer”
- Space is missing after “290,560” in second line of Introduction section
- “Imagenet” -> “ImageNet”
- “challenging” -> “challenge”, third line in sect. 2.1
- Title of sect 2.2, “Dempester-Shafter” -> “Dempster–Shafer”
- For the sake of completion, the first index of the sum should be given in Eqn (1), I assume it’s k=1, as the sum over alphas goes from k=1 to K also after Eqn (2)
- Capitalize CUDA in sect. 4
- “each pre-trained models” to “each pre-trained model” in sect. 5.1 
- It should say that the figures 4&5 are in the appendix which are referenced in sect 6
- Appendix A, Eqn (6), define the operator used
- Appendix A, “Kullback libeler” -> “Kullback–Leibler”
- Appendix A, the definition of KL: In the log-term, I assume the K should be above the product sign, rather then a term index by a Gamma function
- Appendix A, in the following line, the operator should be defined, I assume a Hadamard product?
- Appendix B, broken figure reference
- Appendix B, “visualizations are not sometimes…”
- Appendix B, Fig 4, capitalize “saliency”
content.summary_of_the_review: The study addresses a relevant problem of early vs. late fusion of input features, however the current paper requires significant adjustments to improve the clarity of what conclusions can be drawn from the evaluated experiments, the presented numerical results need to be checked and the paper lacks novelty in terms of representation learning to be relevant for the ICLR audience.

content.title: MULTI-VIEW DEEP EVIDENTIAL FUSION NEURAL NETWORK FOR ASSESSMENT OF SCREENING MAMMOGRAMS
content.abstract:
Mammography is an X-ray-based imaging technique widely used for breast cancer screening and early-risk assessment. A large number of mammograms are acquired in regular breast cancer screening programs. The assessment of mammograms is a tedious task and may be difficult to accomplish due to a shortage of expert radiologists in breast imaging. Artificial intelligence-powered algorithms, especially deep learning, could assist radiologists by automating the assessment, however, substantial trust needs to be established in incorporating such algorithms in real-world settings. The evidential neural networks algorithm provides an interpretable approach using Dempster-Shafter evidential theory that supports network predictive confidence. Recent studies have suggested that multi-view analysis improves the assessment of mammograms. In this study, we advance the multi-view assessment of mammograms by using a deep evidential neural network to address the following questions:

1. What is the effect of various pre-trained convolutional neural networks in extracting features from mammograms?
2. Which fusion strategies work better for the multi-view assessment of mammograms using a deep evidential learning framework?

The multi-view deep evidential neural network extracts features from each mammogram’s view using a pre-trained convolutional neural network. The extracted features are combined using Dempster-Shafer evidence theory for the following two classification tasks, mammogram density assessment in BI-RADS categories and mammogram finding as benign or malignant. We conducted extensive experiments using two open-sourced digital mammogram datasets, VinDr-mammo, and mini-DDSM, with 4,977 and 1,885 patients, each with four mammogram views, respectively. The results suggest that the multi-view approach outperforms the single-view by relative improvements of 2.99% and 2.64% for VinDr-mammo, and 6.51% and 8.75% for mini-DDSM datasets, in terms of F1-score, in mammogram density assessment and BI-RADS findings benign/malignant classification tasks, respectively. Our results show that the multi-view assessment of mammograms using a deep evidential fusion approach not only provides superior performance than the single-view assessment but also enhances trust in incorporating artificial intelligence-powered algorithms for the assessment of screening mammograms.
